line: It’s Young Wunna and Young Wheezy, man, this shit too easy
vault_lines: It's Young Wunna and Young Wheezy, man, this shit too easy
meaning:
“too easy” is one of countless tracks that establish and accentuate Gunna and Wheezy as a remarkable rapper and producer duo. This song’s chorus highlights Wheezy’s consistency with production, similar to Gunna’s 2019 release, “3 Headed Snake”—its opening line sang by Young Thug boasting:

Shit, me, Gunna, and Wheezy, that’s a three-headed snake

Gunna and NAV dedicated a track to their frequent collaborator in November, 2020, titled “Young Wheezy.” The song begins and ends with Gunna repeating Wheezy’s trademark nickname of “Young Wheezy,” similar to how Gunna has adopted the moniker of “Young Wunna.”

The pair have over a hundred collaborations between their discographies. In an interview with COMPLEX following Gunna’s 2020 project, WUNNA, Wheezy said this about the success the album:

My favorite song from Gunna [on the album] is “GIMMICK.” [When WUNNA went No. 1], I was expecting it for sure. But for the last album, Drip or Drown 2, to do what it did, and then see the growth for this year for WUNNA was crazy. Because the last album went No. 2. And then this year, to see the growth and we was No. 1, man, it was just a relief knowing that the music is catching up with the time… [Gunna] is my best friend. We been friends forever.

The consistency and effortless teamwork between the pair causes the duo to stand out from others in the rap game. Wheezy and Gunna’s chemistry continually is apparent given their collaborative streak of successful records.

line: Another check came in, God, forgive my sins

Every check reminds him that his lifestyle is built on sin. He’s rich but he’s guilty.

This is that Atlanta church kid in him. Gunna grew up in the church. His mom is very religious. So even when he gets a $500k check, his first thought is “Lord forgive me.”

It’s also that classic trapper guilt – you want the money, but you know God is watching how you got it.

That’s why this line is so cold. Most rappers would say “Another check came in, I’m blessed.” Gunna says “Another check came in… forgive me.”

He knows the money and the sins come together.

line: I could tell you ’bout the time I counted an M in a night I could tell you ’bout the time I fucked me a dime on a flight
vault_lines: I could tell you 'bout the time
meaning:
These two go together – one about money, one about women – back to back flex but it’s deeper.

M = Million dollars.

Gunna is not exaggerating. In 2021-2022 at his peak, off shows alone he was getting $150k-$250k per show, plus streams, plus features ($100k per feature), plus merch. On a big night with a festival + 2 club walkthroughs, yeah he can touch an M in one night.

“counted” – He says counted, not made. Because making it is digital now, but counting it cash is that old Southside trap feeling. He grew up counting small bills, now he’s counting 7 figures in one night. Full circle.

“I could tell you ‘bout the time I fucked me a dime on a flight”

Dime = perfect 10.

On a flight = This is that private jet / first class life. Mile High Club type shit.

But Gunna’s wordplay: “I fucked me a dime on a flight"could also mean he met her on a flight and fucked, or he flew a dime out to fuck. Both happen when you’re rich.

Why he puts these two lines together: He’s showing you the extreme highs of his life. One night you’re counting a million dollars cash, next hour you’re smashing a 10/10 on a jet.

That’s the life he prayed for when he was broke on the Southside.
But remember the rest of the song is about losses, fights, almost giving up. He’s saying yeah I lived the crazy highs too, but the highs don’t erase the lows.

line: I could tell you ’bout the money, cars, and hoes, and the ice
vault_lines: I could tell you 'bout the money, cars, and hoes, and the ice
meaning:
This is classic Gunna flex, but on this song it’s not bragging – it’s like he’s tired of it.

Breakdown:

“money, cars, and hoes, and the ice” – That’s the rap starter pack. Every rapper talks about it. Gunna literally has it all:
- Money: $15M+ net worth off just music, no 360 deal
- Cars: Maybach, Lambo Urus, Rolls Royce Cullinan, he collects them
- Hoes: He dated Chloe Bailey, he has his pick
- Ice: His Peter Marco chains, $500k Patek watches, flooded Audemars

But the way he says “I could tell you ‘bout” – he’s saying it like yeah, I got it, but what does it even mean?

On WUNNA Gunna would say money cars hoes ice and be excited. On Bittersweet / The Time era Gunna says it like it’s just normal to him now. It’s not making him happy anymore.

He’s realized all that stuff didn’t save him from:
- Jail
- Losing friends
- Depression
- Being alone in a mansion

So this line is him checking off the boxes – “yeah I got the money, cars, hoes, ice… but I also got wins and losses, times we almost gave up…”

He’s showing you the ice is real, but the pain behind it is realer.

line: I could tell you ’bout the time we ain’t give up and we still fight
vault_lines: I could tell you 'bout the time we ain't give up and we still fight
meaning:
This is the most important line in that whole run.

“we” – Notice he stopped saying “I” and now says “we”. This is not just Gunna. This is YSL. This is him and Thug, him and his day-one friends from Southside, him and Turbo. His real circle.

“ain’t give up” – There were so many moments they could have quit:
- When Gunna was broke sleeping on floors in College Park in 2016
- When Drip Season 1 flopped and nobody cared
- When the whole city turned on him in 2022-2023 and said “Gunna is canceled”
- When Thug was facing life in jail

They didn’t quit.

“we still fight” – Present tense. Even right now, in 2024-till today when he made Bittersweet and One of Wun, they are still fighting. Fighting the case, fighting depression, fighting to stay #1.

It’s not past tense like “we fought”. It’s “we STILL fight”.

Gunna is saying resilience is his real drip. The chains, the clothes are nothing – the real flex is that after everything – RICO, betrayal, lost millions – he and his few real ones are still standing and still fighting for the spot.

That’s why fans fuck with Gunna heavy after the case. He didn’t give up.

line: I could tell you ’bout the wins and all the losses in my life
vault_lines: I could tell you 'bout the wins and all the losses in my life
meaning:
This is Gunna in his reflective bag, like Bittersweet / a Gift & a Curse era Gunna.

“wins” – For him:
- Going from selling weed in College Park to #1 album WUNNA
- Drip Too Hard went Diamond (10 million)
- Buying his mom a house, buying Maybachs
- Surviving the YSL case and coming home in 2022

“all the losses” -
- Losing friends who switched on him and called him a rat
- Losing Thug for a minute when Thug went to jail
- Losing relationships cause his trust is fucked up
- Losing money on drugs, lawyers, fake friends

What makes this line hard is the “all” – he’s not just gonna tell you the wins like most rappers. Most rappers only flex. Gunna is saying if I really told you my life story, I’d have to tell you the losses too.

And he lost a lot. In 2023 he said in interviews he was depressed, couldn’t sleep, lost 30 lbs from stress.

But he says “I could tell you” – meaning he could, but he won’t go into detail. He keeps it vague on purpose. He lets the music speak instead of doing interviews and explaining every loss.

That’s why that whole run of music hits different – he’s not just rapping about drip anymore, he’s rapping about wins AND losses.

line: I could tell you ’bout the time I made a call and we got it right
vault_lines: I could tell you 'bout the time I made a call and we got it right
meaning:
This is Gunna talking about real street/business decisions where one phone call changed everything.

“I could tell you ‘bout the time” – He’s about to give you a war story, but he doesn’t give you all the details on purpose. Gunna never snitches on himself in lyrics. He gives you just enough.

“I made a call” – In Gunna’s world a “call” is never just a phone call. A call can mean:
- Call to his plug to get a play
- Call to Thug to get on a song
- Call to his lawyer when the case hit
- Call to his shooter / his manager / his jeweler – one call and things move.

He is the type of n***a where one call fixes everything. That’s power.

“and we got it right” – That call WORKED. It wasn’t a failed play. He called, the money came, the feature came, the case got handled, the hit came.

Why he says it like that: He’s showing you he’s not lucky, he’s connected and decisive. He doesn’t sit and stress, he makes the call and the team executes and they get it right – the profit, the escape, the win.

It’s also why on a lot of Gunna songs he says “I made a call” right before success – because in his life, one phone call really did take him from College Park trap to chart-topper.

vault_lines: I told you I wasn't just a John Doe (John Doe)
meaning:
In the United States, John Doe (and the female counterpart Jane Doe) is a placeholder name used when a person’s real identity is unknown or must be withheld.

It’s commonly used in:

Law enforcement and courts – for suspects, victims, or parties in a case whose names are not yet known (“John Doe #3”).

Hospitals – for unidentified or unconscious patients without ID.

Legal and educational examples – as a generic stand-in for “the average person” (similar to “John Smith” or “Joe Public”).

The term originates from medieval English law, where “John Doe” was a fictional plaintiff name used in legal cases to represent an unknown party.

1) “The stick” look up “stick talk” by Future.
 This slang is in reference to an automatic rifle in Southern hip-hop in the U.S. That means you can “stick ‘em up”

2) “Mister X”- As of lately some prominent names referred to as ‘X’ surrounding the hip hop culture includes, but not limited to, XXX Tentacion & DMX. But Gunna is referring to Malcolm X hence the next line

3) “That’s by any means” On June 28, 1964 Malcolm X spoke at the founding rally of the Organization of Afro-American Unity in New York. He called for freedom, justice, and equality “by any means necessary.” This itself was a translation of a phrase used by Martinican intellectual Frantz Fanon in his 1960 Address to the Accra Positive Action Conference, “Why we use violence”.

The phrase had also been used by French intellectual Jean-Paul Sartre in his play Dirty Hands in 1948.

In May of 2022, Gunna was arrested and charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act. He and Young Thug were arrested along with twenty-six other individuals as part of a grand jury indictment that named their affiliation to YSL (Young Slime or Stoner Life) as criminal street gang activity. The indictment alleges that YSL, under the leadership of Thug, engaged in murder, armed robbery, and witness intimidation, among other illegal acts in furtherance of the gang.

In December of 2022, Gunna was released from jail after entering into an Alford plea agreement, admitting to YSL’s status as a criminal street gang while also expressing his innocence. Several members accepted plea deals as well, including YSL co-founder Walter Murphy and artists Lil Duke and  Slimelife Shawty.

Following this guilty plea, Gunna has been widely accused of being a snitch, particularly following the release of leaked video from his Alford plea proceeding. At the time of release of “bread & butter,” Young Thug remains behind bars and faces the possibility of life in prison.

Despite the accusations, Gunna maintains his innocence and insists that he would never inform on his friends. While it is unlikely that Gunna will testify against YSL members in court, his admission of YSL’s status as a criminal street gang can be used against Thug and other defendants that did not enter into plea agreements.

Lean is a concoction that has become popular in recent years. The first ingredient is cough syrup, which contains codeine, and may also have promethazine, an antihistamine. That is then added to a soda (typically sprite) and could have jolly ranchers to add flavor.

Codeine is an opioid that is commonly used in cough syrup to suppress any minor sickness. Opioid drugs are known for being highly addictive substances that should only be taken in moderation to compensate for pain. Abuse of these drugs, especially if not prescribed, can lead memory loss, headaches, blurred vision and dizziness in the short term and tooth decay, weight gain, irregular heart rate and seizures in the long term.

The beginning stages after going long periods without codeine, once addicted, are anxiety, muscle aches, sweating and increased heart and breathing rate. The later withdrawals include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal cramping.

Because Gunna’s new partner vastly differs from his previous girl in her lack of desire to leech off of his money and fame and her willingness to have frequent sex, he praises her and makes it clear that she is a significant upgrade from his past relationship.

line: Show’s around one-fifty, but they paid a lil’ more (More)
vault_lines: Show's around one-fifty, but they paid a lil' more (More)
meaning:
This line from Gunna can be interpreted in numerous ways. He says that his “show’s around one-fifty”, which can be referring to the time of day of his show: 1:50 in the afternoon or in the middle of the night. However, the following statement, “they paid a lil' more”, implies that the fans attending the aforementioned show paid slightly more than 150 dollars as an entry fee. This hints that the “one-fifty” that Gunna used to describe his show may be referring to the price of tickets ($150) rather than the time that the show is scheduled for.
Additionally, the “one-fifty” that was paid could be interpreted as what was paid directly to Gunna, in which case he would likely be hinting that he was paid $150,000 to do a show. This, however, is a less likely explanation, given that Gunna typically makes around $30,000 for each performance. But rappers embellish all the time in their lyrics, so maybe Gunna does the same here in “Blindfold”.
